issues.legal_issue: Time spent pursuing a civil revision may be excluded when the later suit seeks to establish possession rights after an execution order and the revisional court was unable, for a cause comparable to lack of jurisdiction, to determine those rights.
material_facts: After an execution court rejected the objector’s claim to possession, the objector pursued a civil revision instead of filing the suit available to establish his claimed possession rights.

The High Court entertained the revision, but the nature of the execution proceedings and the conclusive effect of the execution court’s order, subject to a fresh suit, meant that the High Court could not determine the parties’ rights on facts in the revision.
The earlier proceeding was pursued with due diligence and was based on the same cause of action as the later suit.
The objector filed the later suit after the revision was dismissed.
issues.conclusion: The revisional court was unable to entertain the proceeding for a cause comparable to a defect of jurisdiction, so the time spent in the revision could be excluded under Section 14, provided the other statutory conditions, including good faith, were met.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908 allows exclusion of time spent prosecuting with due diligence and in good faith another civil proceeding founded on the same cause of action where the court was unable to entertain it because of a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature. Under the pre-amendment scheme of Order 21, Rules 97–103 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an execution court conducted a summary inquiry into obstruction, and a person other than the judgment-debtor whose claim was rejected could bring a fresh suit to establish possession rights; the execution order was otherwise conclusive. Article 11A of the Limitation Act prescribed the limitation period for that suit. The Court distinguished the Patna High Court decision reported at AIR 1994 Patna 225 because there the litigant had been cautioned that the appeal was not maintainable, whereas here the revision was entertained for hearing.

rule.if: possession_rights_suit_after_execution_order and diligent_prior_civil_proceeding and same_cause_of_action and prior_court_unable_to_determine_rights and good_faith

predicates.possession_rights_suit_after_execution_o: A person who is not the judgment-debtor brings a civil suit to establish claimed possession rights after an execution court has rejected the person’s objection to an execution-related claim to possession.
predicates.diligent_prior_civil_proceeding: The person pursued the earlier civil proceeding with due diligence.
predicates.same_cause_of_action: The earlier civil proceeding and the later suit were founded on the same cause of action.
predicates.prior_court_unable_to_determine_rights: The earlier court could not determine the parties’ substantive rights because the nature of the proceeding or a comparable procedural limitation prevented it from doing so.
predicates.good_faith: The person prosecuted the earlier proceeding with due care and attention.

issues.definition: When a person brings a suit to establish possession rights after an execution order, and diligently and in good faith pursued an earlier proceeding based on the same cause, time spent in that proceeding is excluded if the earlier court could not determine the substantive rights.

issues.legal_issue: A litigant may prosecute a civil revision in good faith despite having chosen an unsuitable remedy on counsel’s advice, where the litigant exercised due care in the circumstances.
material_facts: The objector was illiterate and not legally trained.
The objector filed the revision on the advice of counsel rather than filing the suit available to establish possession rights.
The High Court entertained the revision for hearing, giving the objector reason to expect that the execution order might be set aside.
There was uncertainty at the time about the availability of revision in such circumstances, and there was no inordinate delay in filing the later suit.
The Court found no lack of due care by the objector.
issues.conclusion: The objector prosecuted the revision in good faith and could not be denied the benefit of Section 14 merely because counsel had advised an unsuitable remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(h) of the Limitation Act, 1908 defines good faith by requiring due care and attention. Due care depends on the circumstances and means that sufficient care was taken and there was no negligence. Although proceeding contrary to a clearly expressed legal provision may indicate a lack of good faith, that principle is not to be applied rigidly in every case. The Court considered the litigant’s lack of legal training, reliance on counsel’s advice, the High Court’s decision to entertain the revision, and the absence of inordinate delay.

rule.if: civil_revision_after_execution_objection and litigant_not_legally_trained and counsel_advised_revision and revision_entertained_for_hearing and procedural_uncertainty and no_inordinate_delay

predicates.civil_revision_after_execution_objection: A litigant pursues a civil revision after an execution court rejects the litigant’s objection to a claim for possession.
predicates.litigant_not_legally_trained: The litigant is illiterate or otherwise not legally trained.
predicates.counsel_advised_revision: The litigant pursues the revision on counsel’s advice rather than from a deliberate disregard of the proper remedy.
predicates.revision_entertained_for_hearing: The revisional court entertains the revision for hearing instead of rejecting it at the outset as unavailable.
predicates.procedural_uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the relevant legal practice about whether revision is an available remedy in the circumstances.
predicates.no_inordinate_delay: The litigant does not cause inordinate delay before bringing the later suit.

issues.definition: A litigant who is not legally trained and follows counsel’s advice may have prosecuted a revision in good faith when the court entertains it, the availability of that remedy is uncertain, and the later suit is not brought after inordinate delay.
